Founder Story · Leadership

Nothing Is Lost. Only Gained.

What building a business has taught me about leadership, teamwork, staying curious and bringing people with us as AI changes the way we work.

LW
Lisa WarrenFounder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI · 4 November 2026 · 6 min read
Lisa WarrenFounder & CEO

I have always had an entrepreneurial streak. I inherited much of that from my father: the instinct to spot an opportunity, ask questions, find a way forward and never be too comfortable with the status quo. It has been part of me throughout my career, whether I was working inside an organisation, leading a team, building a strategy or starting something of my own.

Starting Neural Horizons AI gave me the opportunity to put that instinct into practice in a very different way. Building a business from the ground up teaches you things you cannot learn from a job description. You become responsible for the vision, the decisions, the relationships, the delivery and all the details in between. You learn to be resourceful, resilient and comfortable making decisions when there is no established playbook.

It has been challenging, exciting and an enormous learning experience. And it has reinforced something important: I haven't lost anything by taking the entrepreneurial route. I have gained another layer of experience, perspective and capability that I will carry into whatever comes next.

“Entrepreneurship isn't a job title. It's a mindset I will carry with me throughout my career.”

Lisa Warren

The part of leadership I miss most

There is one part of working in an organisation that I genuinely miss: the people. I miss leading and developing a team, working alongside other leaders, sharing ideas around a table and seeing what happens when different strengths come together around a common goal.

I miss the conversations that challenge your thinking, the energy of a team working through a difficult problem, the moments when someone grows into a responsibility they once thought was beyond them, and the shared satisfaction of delivering something meaningful together.

As a founder, you can build a network and collaborate with brilliant people, but it is not quite the same as being part of a team with shared ownership, shared momentum and a common direction. That experience has reminded me how much I value people leadership and the contribution that strong teams make to a business.

“One of the greatest lessons in leadership is knowing your strengths – and knowing who you need beside you.”

Lisa Warren

Knowing what you bring — and staying curious

I have spent more than 20 years working across digital, commercial strategy, marketing, business development and transformation. I love strategic thinking: understanding what a business is trying to achieve, seeing the connections others may miss, asking the uncomfortable questions and turning an idea into a practical plan.

I still love marketing, too. Not simply the campaigns or the communications, but the thinking behind it: understanding customers, behaviour, markets, positioning and what makes people choose one solution over another. That curiosity has always been part of how I approach business.

AI has opened up another extraordinary area to explore. I am passionate about where it is going and, more importantly, what it can make possible for organisations. I do not pretend to be an engineer or to know every technical discipline in depth. I believe in being honest about what I know, continuing to learn, asking good questions and working with the right technical people to turn business needs into solutions that work.

My strength is connecting the business challenge to the opportunity: understanding the process, the people, the data and the outcome that matters, then helping bring the right expertise together to make progress. That is where strategy and technology need to meet.

AI is moving quickly. People need to come with it.

Keeping up with AI and understanding where it is taking us is becoming essential. The pace of change is remarkable. New models, tools, agents and capabilities are emerging constantly. It is important to follow the developments, understand what is genuinely useful, question the hype and translate what is happening into something relevant to the organisation.

But there is a part of AI adoption that I believe deserves just as much attention as the technology itself: the people who will work alongside it.

Employees should not be left to guess what AI means for their roles, or be expected to embrace tools they have not been shown how to use. When leaders communicate poorly, uncertainty grows. When people are excluded from the conversation, they can feel that change is happening to them rather than with them.

Organisations need to be transparent. Explain what is being introduced and why. Be clear about what AI can and cannot do. Provide training, reliable information and opportunities to experiment safely. Invite employees to identify repetitive tasks, process frustrations and areas where better tools could help them do their jobs more effectively.

This is not about pretending that work will never change. It will. It is about helping people understand that change, giving them the opportunity to build new skills and making sure they have a voice in how it happens. A culture of curiosity and continuous learning will be far better prepared than one built around fear or avoidance.

⬡ A leadership responsibility

AI adoption starts with people, not technology. Leaders have to understand the change well enough to explain it, make space for questions and bring their teams along.

What comes next

I am proud of what I have built with Neural Horizons AI and the practical work it has allowed me to do. The experience has stretched me, strengthened my commercial judgement and deepened my understanding of how AI can be applied to real business challenges.

It has also made me clearer about the kind of work that energises me: bringing people together, shaping strategy, solving problems, developing teams and helping organisations navigate change. I want to keep learning, keep building and keep contributing — ideally alongside people who are as curious, ambitious and collaborative as I am.

Being entrepreneurial does not mean having to build everything alone. It means bringing initiative, ownership and a willingness to make things happen wherever you are. Those qualities are just as valuable inside an organisation as they are when you are building one.

“I haven't lost my entrepreneurial spirit. I've strengthened it. And I have even more to contribute.”

Lisa Warren

Nothing is lost. Only gained.

If there is one thing I know, it is that every chapter adds something. The next one should build on everything that came before — the experience, the lessons, the people and the ambition to keep moving forward.

Let's keep the conversation going.

Whether you are exploring AI adoption, building a team or thinking about what leadership looks like in a changing business environment, I would love to connect.
